At work we have a vending machine full of candy and I've noticed lately I've been getting candy more frequently than normal and began to worry I might have a sugar addiction. Reading this article confirmed that I do have a sugar addiction lol.

So, a while back I dabbled in keto. For those unfamiliar, it's near-total abstention from carbohydrates in any form - sugars, starches, etc. I'll leave aside the benefits and drawbacks for a more relevant conversation, but suffice to say I didn't eat sugar or things that metabolized into sugar for several months. This is what I observed during and after that time:

  • Things are SWEET. If you go without for a while, you start to taste sugar in things you didn't think about as sweet before. When having a cheat beer, slice of bread or other predominantly grainy/starchy thing I'd have a sweet taste in my mouth afterwards. Fruit is incredible, soda is unbearable. I haven't been able to drink soda even having been off keto for a long while, it's just too much.

  • Bitter is not terrible. Operating without sugar allowed me to develop a greater tolerance for things with biting or bitter flavors, and I've grown to appreciate a lot of them for the deeper, richer flavors that they have. Unsweetened chocolate used to make me gag, but it became a favorite snack during the time I was doing keto and I still enjoy it. Black coffee doesn't even register as bitter for me, and a campari and soda went from deadly poison to nice treat.

  • Starch is insidious. Noticing the simple carbs everywhere really gets you thinking about what you're putting into your body. Metabolically speaking, a slice of white bread is little different from an equivalent nutritional quantity of table sugar. Simple carbs are in EVERYTHING. Read your nutritional labels.

I don't eschew carbs like I used to, but I'm definitely more aware of how hyperaddicted our default diet makes us to the satisfaction of quick starches and sugars. You don't have to do keto like I did, but try this - check out the nutrition of everything you eat in a day and tally up everything in the carbs column. Try to keep it under 100g, and notice how hard that is. 100g! That's not a small amount, but it's trivially easy to exceed with most food.

How does one even avoid sugar? The article seemed to express this as a pretty difficult task, which I can believe quite easily.

What did you eat, and how out of the way did you have to go to avoid sugars?

It's not something you can do without thinking about it, but it's not as hard as you might think. I would normally either skip breakfast or eat something high-fat (bit of cheese was a good go-to), then demolish a really big salad with meat on it for lunch. I eat out a lot because of where I work, so my usual suspects were chipotle salads (skip the dressing), jimmy john's lettuce wraps, greek salads with lots of feta and chicken, things like that. Greens with meat was the order of the day. Dinner was normally a smaller meal, but generally I was looking at meats, cheeses, maybe another salad, some nuts to vary it up.

The thing that was most surprising is that I was NEVER hungry. Maybe if I went most of a day without eating I'd feel something, but I didn't get that intense "wow, I should eat" craving I was used to. More of a gentle reminder that I hadn't eaten in a while. It was much less intense and made it easier to take my time to prep a meal rather than diving in for immediate sustenance.

Worst part is that there's only so many sources of non-meat fat. Nuts are the thing you'd think of immediately, but it turns out they have a surprising amount of carbs so they're a no-go in large quantities. Avocados are a godsend, but they're really crappy when out of season and they go bad relatively fast so you have to keep searching for good ones in the store. It's not hard to eat keto, but it's pretty draining to keep your diet varied enough not to get bored.

If you're interested in further info, there's a pretty good reddit community over at r/keto.

If you do try out a ketogenic diet for a week, you should be aware that around day two or three, you'll probably start to feel really weird. Your body will be transitioning from normal blood sugar to ketone bodies for energy, and there are some side effects during that transition. Some people report a couple of days of "garlic breath," for example. A little reading will prevent a lot of surprises. If you do try it out, expect to drop 5-10 pounds in the first week or two.

Cutting out or cutting down on consuming processed foods is probably the first step to reducing hidden sugars. Read the nutrition and ingredient labels, if you haven't gotten into the habit yet, you'll soon realize all sorts of food products have sugars added. Stuff like tomato soup, ketchup, pasta sauces, yogourt, Miracle Whip, and peanut butter are just a few foods that added sugar is sneaking into our diet.
